triage.name: Insomnia
triage.reason: Common sleep complaint reachable by history and medication/substance review; a good interview-driven case with psychiatric and medical mimics.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'polysomnography (sleep study)' was in ['supporting', 'not_indicated'], kept ['not_indicated', 'supporting']
auto-repaired: workup: 'actigraphy (wrist actigraph)' was in ['supporting', 'not_indicated'], kept ['not_indicated', 'supporting']

auto-repaired: workup: 'Polysomnography (sleep study)' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if snoring, witnessed apnea, daytime sleepiness, or treatment-refractory insomnia)

auto-repaired: workup: 'Actigraphy (wrist actigraph)' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if circadian rhythm disorder or irregular sleep schedule is suspected)
presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common in women than men
Prevalence increases with age, especially in older adults
More common in people with lower income and less stable housing
More common in shift workers and people who travel across time zones
More common in African American adults, who report longer time to fall asleep and poorer sleep quality

risk_factors.text: Ongoing stress or recent major life stressor (job loss, divorce, bereavement)
Depression, anxiety, or other emotional distress

social_history: Shift work or rotating work schedules
Irregular sleep schedule or inconsistent bedtime
Stressful life events or caregiving responsibilities
exposures: Bright light or screen use close to bedtime

chief_complaints.text: I can't fall asleep at night
I wake up in the middle of the night and can't get back to sleep
I wake up way too early and can't go back to sleep
I'm tired all day because I don't sleep well

hpi.onset: Often starts after a stressful event, change in schedule, illness, or new medication; can also begin gradually without a clear trigger
hpi.duration: Acute if less than 1 month; chronic if at least 3 nights per week for 3 months or longer
hpi.progression: May resolve when the trigger passes, or persist and become chronic as worry about sleep and poor sleep habits build
hpi.quality: Difficulty initiating sleep, difficulty maintaining sleep, or early morning awakening; sleep feels unrefreshing
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; measured by how long it takes to fall asleep, how often the patient wakes, total sleep time, and daytime impairment
hpi.timing: At night, at sleep onset, during the night, or in the early morning; daytime symptoms the next day
aggravating: Screen use or bright light before bed
relieving: Good sleep habits and a consistent schedule
Treating the underlying medical or psychiatric problem
Removing the offending medication or substance
pertinent_negatives: Loud snoring or witnessed pauses in breathing
Gasping or choking awake at night
Urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations in the evening
Falling asleep unintentionally during the day, such as while driving
Acting out dreams or injuring self or bed partner during sleep
Severe chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations at night
Fever, night sweats, or weight loss
New focal weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking

positives.text: Tiredness or low energy during the day

argues_against: Primary insomnia when prominent mood or psychotic symptoms are present

atypical.how_it_differs: Sleep is lighter and more fragmented; they often wake early and may not report feeling sleepy during the day even when sleep is poor.
missing_classic_features: Clear difficulty falling asleep at the start of the night

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may resist going to bed, need a parent to fall asleep, or wake and call out at night; daytime irritability and school problems may be the main complaint.
Insomnia is common and often driven by frequent urination, nausea, back pain, fetal movement, and anxiety about the pregnancy or newborn.
missing_classic_features: Primary insomnia without a clear physical trigger

atypical.how_it_differs: Insomnia may coexist with obstructive sleep apnea; snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, and daytime sleepiness are more prominent.
missing_classic_features: Pure sleep-onset insomnia without breathing symptoms

general.mild: Alert, well-appearing, no distress; may look tired with mild periorbital shadowing
general.moderate: Tired-appearing with periorbital darkening, mild psychomotor slowing, yawning; still fully oriented
general.severe: Markedly fatigued, slowed speech and movement, poor attention, appears exhausted
general.critical: Not applicable; insomnia itself does not produce a critical general appearance, and an acutely toxic or obtunded patient should prompt evaluation for another cause

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation
findings.finding: Vital signs are normal; no fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, or hypoxemia

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's general appearance and level of alertness
findings.finding: Fatigued appearance with periorbital darkening, yawning, and mild psychomotor slowing

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx and nares and palpate the neck
findings.finding: No tonsillar hypertrophy, macroglossia, nasal obstruction, or goiter

findings.maneuver: Assess the oropharyngeal airway (Mallampati class) and neck circumference
findings.finding: Crowded oropharynx or increased neck circumference suggesting obstructive sleep apnea

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate peripheral pulses
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lungs and observe the breathing pattern
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without wheezing, crackles, or prolonged expiration
Soft, non-tender, without organomegaly or mass

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including cranial nerves, strength, sensation, coordination, and gait
findings.finding: No focal deficits, tremor, rigidity, or ataxia

findings.maneuver: Assess mood, affect, and screen for depression and anxiety
findings.finding: No prominent depressed mood, anhedonia, or anxiety disorder; mood symptoms, when present, are mild and reactive to poor sleep

findings.maneuver: Ask about and observe for an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations in the evening
findings.finding: No restlessness or leg discomfort at rest

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the lower extremities for edema

labs.caveat: Hyperthyroidism (low TSH) can also cause insomnia; check TSH to rule out thyroid disease as a reversible cause.
Poorly controlled diabetes can cause nocturia and sleep disruption; not a direct cause of insomnia.
Deficiency can cause restless legs and sleep disturbance; consider if diet or malabsorption risk.
Low ferritin is associated with restless legs syndrome, which can fragment sleep.
Only if Cushing syndrome is suspected (e.g., central obesity, striae, hypertension); not routine.

imaging.preferred_when: When obstructive sleep apnea, central sleep apnea, narcolepsy, or periodic limb movements are suspected, or when insomnia is treatment-refractory

findings.text: Increased wake after sleep onset and reduced sleep efficiency
Normal sleep architecture without significant apnea-hypopnea events
Apnea-hypopnea index elevated, suggesting comorbid obstructive sleep apnea

imaging.preferred_when: When sleep-wake pattern is unclear or circadian rhythm disorder is suspected

findings.text: Irregular sleep-wake schedule with variable sleep onset and offset times
Reduced total sleep time and increased nocturnal wakefulness
Normal brain parenchyma; no structural lesion, mass, or stroke

initial.why: Screens for thyroid dysfunction as a reversible medical cause of insomnia
Checks for anemia or infection that could contribute to fatigue and poor sleep
Assesses electrolytes, renal function, and glucose as contributors to sleep disruption

supporting.why: Evaluates for diabetes, which can cause nocturia and sleep fragmentation
supporting.only_if: polyuria, nocturia, or diabetes risk factors are present

supporting.why: Low ferritin is linked to restless legs syndrome
Deficiency can cause restless legs and neurologic symptoms
supporting.only_if: dietary restriction, malabsorption, or paresthesias are present

supporting.why: Screens for Cushing syndrome when clinical features suggest it
supporting.only_if: central obesity, striae, or hypertension raise suspicion for Cushing syndrome

supporting.why: Diagnoses sleep apnea or periodic limb movements when suspected
supporting.only_if: snoring, witnessed apnea, daytime sleepiness, or treatment-refractory insomnia

supporting.why: Clarifies sleep-wake pattern over days to weeks
supporting.only_if: circadian rhythm disorder or irregular sleep schedule is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for focal neurologic findings or suspected structural lesion

decision_points: Diagnosis of insomnia is clinical, based on sleep history and daytime impairment; labs are used to exclude reversible medical causes.
Order TSH in all patients with new or worsening insomnia to rule out thyroid disease.
Consider polysomnography only when sleep apnea, narcolepsy, or periodic limb movements are suspected, or when insomnia is refractory to treatment.
Screen for depression, anxiety, and substance use as they are common contributors to insomnia.

criteria.name: Insomnia disorder (clinical diagnosis)
criteria.summary: Difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, or early morning awakening with daytime impairment, occurring at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months despite adequate opportunity for sleep, and not better explained by another sleep disorder, substance, or medical condition.
items: Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early
Daytime impairment (fatigue, mood disturbance, cognitive difficulties)
Occurs at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months
Not better explained by another sleep disorder, substance, or medical condition

differential.name: Obstructive sleep apnea
differential.why_considered: Fragmented sleep with daytime fatigue and non-restorative sleep is the most common mimic of insomnia, especially in older or heavier adults.
differential.trigger: Loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, or gasping/choking awake at night

history: Daytime sleepiness rather than just fatigue
labs: No specific lab abnormality; used mainly to exclude other causes
imaging: Polysomnography shows an elevated apnea-hypopnea index with oxygen desaturations

differential.name: Restless legs syndrome
differential.why_considered: An urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations in the evening delays sleep onset and fragments sleep.
differential.trigger: Evening or nighttime urge to move the legs relieved by movement

history: Uncomfortable leg sensations worse at rest and in the evening
Symptoms worse in the evening or night
exam: May see periodic limb movements if observed during sleep
labs: Low serum iron or transferrin saturation
imaging: Polysomnography may show periodic limb movements of sleep

differential.name: Major depressive disorder
differential.why_considered: Depression commonly presents with insomnia, especially early morning awakening, and is a leading cause of chronic insomnia.
differential.trigger: Persistent low mood, anhedonia, or early morning awakening with insomnia

history: Depressed mood most of the day
exam: Depressed mood, flat affect, psychomotor retardation or agitation
labs: CBC and BMP to exclude anemia or metabolic causes of fatigue

differential.name: Generalized anxiety disorder
differential.why_considered: Excessive worry and hyperarousal at bedtime cause difficulty falling asleep and frequent awakenings.

history: Excessive, uncontrollable worry most days for at least 6 months

differential.name: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder
differential.why_considered: Shift work, jet lag, or a delayed sleep phase causes insomnia at the desired sleep time with daytime sleepiness.

history: Sleep schedule shifted relative to desired sleep time
Shift work or recent travel across time zones
Sleeps well when allowed to follow own schedule
imaging: Actigraphy shows an irregular or delayed sleep-wake pattern

differential.name: Substance or medication-induced sleep disorder
differential.why_considered: Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stimulants, and many prescription drugs disrupt sleep initiation and maintenance.

history: Caffeine, alcohol, or nicotine use close to bedtime
New or increased dose of a stimulating medication (e.g., prednisone, albuterol, bupropion, stimulants)
Temporal link between substance use and insomnia
labs: Urine drug screen if substance use is suspected

differential.name: Hyperthyroidism
differential.why_considered: Thyroid overactivity causes hyperarousal, palpitations, and insomnia.

labs: Low TSH with elevated free T4 or T3
imaging: Thyroid ultrasound or uptake scan if nodules or Graves disease suspected

differential.name: Chronic pain syndrome
differential.why_considered: Pain from arthritis, neuropathy, or other chronic conditions repeatedly awakens the patient and prevents return to sleep.

history: Pain that awakens the patient at night
Pain worse with certain positions or movement
exam: Focal tenderness, joint deformity, or reduced range of motion
labs: Inflammatory markers if inflammatory arthritis is suspected
No specific lab abnormality for insomnia
imaging: Joint or spine imaging if structural pain is suspected

severity.mild: Sleep-onset or maintenance difficulty on some nights with mild daytime fatigue but preserved function; total sleep time only slightly reduced.
severity.moderate: Difficulty most nights with noticeable daytime fatigue, irritability, and reduced concentration; some impairment in work or social function.
severity.severe: Nightly insomnia with marked daytime impairment, poor concentration, mood disturbance, and significant distress or functional decline.
severity.critical: Not applicable; insomnia itself is not life-threatening, but severe sleep deprivation from another cause (e.g., mania, delirium, stimulant toxicity) should prompt urgent evaluation.

red_flags.meaning: Major depression or another psychiatric emergency; requires immediate safety assessment and referral.

red_flags.finding: Decreased need for sleep with elevated mood, grandiosity, or increased activity
red_flags.meaning: Suggests mania or hypomania rather than primary insomnia; needs urgent psychiatric evaluation.

red_flags.finding: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, or gasping arousals
red_flags.meaning: Suggests obstructive sleep apnea; refer for sleep study.

red_flags.finding: Falling asleep unintentionally while driving or during activities
red_flags.meaning: Severe daytime sleepiness; evaluate for sleep apnea, narcolepsy, or other sleep disorder and advise against driving.

red_flags.finding: Acting out dreams or injuring self or bed partner during sleep
red_flags.meaning: Suggests REM sleep behavior disorder; refer for polysomnography and neurologic evaluation.

red_flags.finding: New focal neurologic deficits, severe headache, or confusion
red_flags.meaning: Suggests structural neurologic or acute medical cause; urgent workup needed.

complications.name: Motor vehicle or workplace accidents from drowsiness
Worsening of comorbid medical or psychiatric conditions

special_populations.differences: Sleep is lighter and more fragmented; early morning awakening is common; higher risk of falls and cognitive effects from sedative-hypnotics, so behavioral therapy is preferred.
May present with bedtime resistance, needing a parent to fall asleep, or nighttime awakenings; daytime irritability and school problems may dominate; behavioral interventions are first-line.
Insomnia is common and often driven by frequent urination, nausea, back pain, fetal movement, and anxiety; avoid most sedative-hypnotics and prioritize behavioral measures.
Higher likelihood of comorbid obstructive sleep apnea; screen for snoring and witnessed apneas and consider polysomnography.

key_questions.question: What exactly happens when you try to sleep — do you have trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, waking too early, or a mix?
key_questions.looking_for: Sleep-onset, sleep-maintenance, or early-morning-awakening pattern; guides the differential and treatment

key_questions.question: How many nights a week does this happen, and for how long has it been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: At least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months defines chronic insomnia; under 1 month is acute

key_questions.question: How long does it take you to fall asleep, how many times do you wake, and how many hours of sleep do you get in total?
key_questions.looking_for: Objective sleep measures that quantify severity and track response to treatment

key_questions.question: How does this affect you during the day — fatigue, concentration, mood, or falling asleep while driving?
key_questions.looking_for: Daytime impairment, which is required for the diagnosis; unintentional sleepiness while driving is a red flag

key_questions.question: Do you have enough time and a good place to sleep, or is something keeping you from sleeping?
key_questions.looking_for: Adequate opportunity for sleep; if not, the problem may be insufficient sleep opportunity rather than insomnia

key_questions.question: What is your sleep schedule like — bedtime, wake time, and is it the same on workdays and days off?
key_questions.looking_for: Irregular or delayed sleep-wake schedule suggesting a circadian rhythm disorder

key_questions.question: Do you snore loudly, has anyone seen you stop breathing or gasp or choke awake at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Obstructive sleep apnea, the most important mimic; if present, refer for a sleep study

key_questions.question: In the evening or at night, do you feel an urge to move your legs or have uncomfortable leg sensations that get better when you move?
key_questions.looking_for: Restless legs syndrome, which delays sleep onset and fragments sleep

key_questions.question: How much caffeine, alcohol, and nicotine do you use, and when during the day or evening?
key_questions.looking_for: Caffeine late in the day, evening alcohol, or nicotine as reversible causes of insomnia

key_questions.question: What do you do in the hour before bed — screens, work, exercise, or worrying about not sleeping?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor sleep habits and conditioned arousal that maintain insomnia and respond to CBT-I

key_questions.question: Do you nap during the day, and how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Daytime napping that reduces homeostatic sleep drive and worsens nighttime insomnia

key_questions.question: Have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless, or lost interest in things you used to enjoy?
key_questions.looking_for: Major depressive disorder, a leading cause of chronic insomnia, especially with early morning awakening

key_questions.question: Do you feel anxious or worried much of the time, or have racing thoughts at bedtime?
key_questions.looking_for: Generalized anxiety disorder or hyperarousal causing sleep-onset insomnia

key_questions.question: Have you had thoughts of hurting yourself or that you would be better off dead?
key_questions.looking_for: Suicidal ideation requiring immediate safety assessment and psychiatric referral

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a period of several days with very little need for sleep, feeling unusually energetic or elevated, or doing things out of character?
key_questions.looking_for: Mania or hypomania, where decreased need for sleep is a core symptom and not primary insomnia

key_questions.question: Do you act out your dreams — kicking, punching, or jumping out of bed — or has your bed partner noticed this?
key_questions.looking_for: REM sleep behavior disorder; refer for polysomnography and neurologic evaluation

key_questions.question: What medications and supplements do you take, including any new or recently increased ones?
key_questions.looking_for: Stimulating medications such as prednisone, albuterol, levothyroxine, bupropion, SSRIs, or stimulants that can cause insomnia

key_questions.question: Do you use any over-the-counter sleep aids, alcohol, cannabis, or other substances to help you sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Self-medication, tolerance, or dependence that may be maintaining the insomnia

key_questions.question: Do you have any medical conditions that wake you at night — pain, trouble breathing, heartburn, needing to urinate, hot flashes, or palpitations?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbid medical causes of sleep disruption such as chronic pain, GERD, BPH, heart failure, COPD, or menopause

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have trouble sleeping, restless legs, or a sleep disorder?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of restless legs syndrome or other sleep disorders

key_questions.question: Do you work nights or rotating shifts, or have you traveled across time zones recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Shift work or jet lag causing a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder

reasoning_points: Difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, or early morning awakening with daytime impairment
Symptoms occur at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months for chronic insomnia, or less than 1 month for acute insomnia
Adequate opportunity for sleep is present, distinguishing insomnia from insufficient sleep opportunity
Daytime consequences such as fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, or mood disturbance are present
Look-alikes are excluded: obstructive sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder, and substance- or medication-induced sleep disruption
Contributing psychiatric conditions such as major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, or mania are screened for
Reversible medical causes such as hyperthyroidism, chronic pain, nocturia, and medication side effects are considered
The diagnosis is clinical, based on sleep history; labs and sleep studies are used to exclude other causes rather than to confirm insomnia

easy: Middle-aged or older adult with a clear story of lying awake at night and daytime fatigue
Symptoms most nights for months with no snoring, leg restlessness, or shift work
Clear temporal link to a stressor or a new stimulating medication
Normal physical exam with no red flags
medium: Insomnia with comorbid depression or anxiety, making it hard to tell which came first
Older adult with early morning awakening and multiple medical conditions
Patient using alcohol or over-the-counter sleep aids that are maintaining the problem
Shift worker with an irregular sleep schedule that mimics insomnia
hard: Insomnia coexisting with obstructive sleep apnea, where snoring and witnessed apneas are subtle
Restless legs syndrome presenting mainly as difficulty falling asleep without volunteered leg symptoms
Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder mistaken for insomnia because the patient sleeps well on their own schedule
Medication-induced insomnia from a recently started or increased drug
Insomnia as the presenting symptom of mania or hypomania, where decreased need for sleep is the key clue
